chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn Al-Mukhtar, and Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn Al-Hasan Al-Alawi, all together from Al-Fath ibn Yazid Al-Jurjani, from Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:
'I wrote to him (peace be upon him) asking him about the skins of the dead (animal) whose meat is (permissible to) eat if it is properly slaughtered.'

So he wrote: 'One may not benefit from a dead (animal) by [using] its skin nor its sinew; but everything that was from the young animals — from the wool if it is sheared, and the hair, and the fur, and the rennet, and the horn — and do not exceed to other than these, God willing.'

key_terms.إِهَاب: ihab — the raw/untanned hide/skin of an animal
key_terms.السِّخَال: al-sikhal — young animals, typically lambs or kids (goats)
key_terms.الْإِنْفَحَة: al-infaha — rennet; the stomach enzyme used to curdle milk for cheese-making
key_terms.الْمَيْتَة: maytah — a dead animal that was not properly ritually slaughtered; ritually impure (najis) in Islamic law
key_terms.ذُكِّيَ: dhukki — past passive of tazkiyah; the act of ritual slaughter making an animal permissible
key_terms.عَصَب: asab — sinew, tendon, or connective tissue
key_terms.لَا يُنْتَفَعُ: la yuntafa'u — 'one may not benefit from'; legal prohibition on use/utility

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible in Shia Islam to use the skin, wool, or horn of a dead (maytah) animal?
ai.summary: This narration records a written responsum (fatwa by correspondence) from Imam Abu al-Hasan, likely Imam al-Ridha (peace be upon him), on the permissibility of using parts of a dead animal (maytah) whose species is otherwise halal for consumption. The questioner — Al-Fath ibn Yazid Al-Jurjani, a close companion of the Imam — asked about the hides of such animals. The Imam's written reply establishes a clear jurisprudential ruling: the skin and sinew of a maytah are impermissible to use, but detachable items such as wool, hair, fur, rennet, and horn are exempt when separated from the carcass. This distinction, tied to whether the items were already severed before death, reflects a foundational principle in Shia fiqh regarding ritual purity (tahara) and the impurity of maytah.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Al Mukhtar Bin Muhammad Bin Al Mukhtar, and Muhammad Bin Al Hassan, from Abdullah Bin Al Hassan Al Alawy, altogether from Al Fat’h Bin Yazeed Al Jurjany, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘I wrote to him<sup>asws</sup> asking him<sup>asws</sup> about the skins of the dead whose meat is eaten, if it is clean’.

So he<sup>asws</sup> wrote: ‘Do not benefit from the death with neither the skin nor the backbone, and (benefit from) everything what was from the items from the wool if sheared, and the hair, and the fur, and the rennet, and the horn, and do not exceed to other than these, Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Willing’.
en.sarwar: 6. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar and Muhammad ibn al-Hassan from ‘Abd Allah ibn al- Hassan al-‘Alawiy all from al-Fath ibn Yazid al-Jurjaniy who has said the following:
“I once wrote to abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, asking about the skins of dead animals which are of the edible kind if slaughtered properly.

He (the Imam) wrote in answer, ‘It is not permissible to benefit from the skins of dead animals or sinew (but you can benefit) from items from lambs, like wool even if they are pulled out, hairs, fur and rennet and nothing besides these by the will of Allah.’”
